newsitem.title: CHINA: Taiwan investment in China seen up after gloom.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan investment in China seen up after gloom.

text.p: Taiwanese investment in China is recovering after a year of political squabbles between Taipei and Beijing, and could reach $50 billion within two years, a leading Taiwan businessman in Shanghai said on Monday.

Yang Dazheng, head of the Taiwan Business Association, said in an interview that an improvement in the political atmosphere between Beijing and Taipei had led to an increase in investment which would continue during the second half of 1996.

"In the second half of 1995 and first half of 1996, the political atmosphere was very bad," the Shanghai-based business leader said. "Companies are very sensitive to this and suspended projects that were already approved by the companies and the Taiwan government.
"Now the atmosphere is not so tense, investment has begun to increase," he said. "Bilateral investment is good for both sides. If political differences are not so big, investment will speed up."

Yang put cumulative Taiwan investment in China at $30 billion, with the direct employment of five million people, and said it could reach $50 billion within two years. Other estimates have put the amount at $20 billion since the late 1980s.
The real figure was higher because companies under-reported investment or directed it through third countries, Yang said.

More money was going into manufacturing, especially of electronics, foodstuffs, consumer goods, computers, machinery and petrochemicals and proportionally less into real estate and service companies, like restaurants and karaoke bars, he said.

More and more Taiwan brands, from instant noodles to biscuits, soy sauce, sweets, canned food and soft drinks, are appearing on the shelves of city supermarkets in China, backed by aggressive advertising on television and in the newspapers.

On Thursday in Beijing, China's Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin told Kao Ching-yuan, head of the President Group that is one of the biggest Taiwan investors in China that, no matter what the circumstances, Beijing would protect the proper interests of Taiwan businesses in China.

"The symbolic importance of this meeting was great, because it showed that differences between the two sides will be limited and not cause overall conflict," Yang said, adding that many Chinese leaders had given similar assurances to investors.

He said that about 50 percent of Taiwan ventures in China made money, a success rate slightly higher than in other countries in the region, where Taiwan firms face language barriers and sometimes anti-Chinese feeling.
Taiwan firms are drawn to China by cheap labour, abundant raw materials, a fast-growing market and a common language.
The main problems Taiwan firms face in China are distribution and difficulties in raising capital, Yang said.

Chinese banks will not lend and Taiwan banks are banned from lending to Taiwan-invested projects in China, while foreign banks will only provide short-term credit which is not very useful for long-term factory investment, he said.
A second problem is channels for timely distribution of goods, he said.
